findings.finding_label: Primary political-economy predictor (Model A): Local income inequality on water rate progressivity (UPR at 30,000 gal/month)
findings.outcome_and_polarity: Unit Price Ratio (UPR) at 30,000 gallons monthly = (average total unit price per gallon at 30,000 gal/month) ÷ (average total unit price per gallon at basic 6,000 gal/month), including fixed and volumetric charges (mean = 0.91, SD = 0.38, range 0.2 to 6.52). Higher UPR (> 1.0) indicates a MORE progressive utility tariff structure (shifting unit costs toward high-volume discretionary consumption and away from basic 6,000 gal/month indoor use), which is favorable to relative basic-volume rate equity/affordability design, though it is a utility-level tariff-structure policy ratio rather than a direct measure of household water access or household expenditure burden.

raw_response.headline_result_summary: In a cross-sectional OLS analysis of 1,183 large US drinking water utilities serving >= 40,000 residents (1,055 local government-owned and 134 private investor-owned utilities in the 1,189-utility frame), Switzer and Teodoro (2025) examine determinants of residential water tariff progressivity, measured by the Unit Price Ratio (UPR = average unit price per gallon at 30,000 gal/month divided by average unit price per gallon at 6,000 gal/month, including fixed and volumetric charges). First, local income inequality (mean-to-median income ratio) is positively and significantly associated with tariff progressivity overall (Model A: b = 0.310, p = 0.005) and among local government utilities (Model B: b = 0.332, p = 0.005). Second, private investor-owned utilities regulated by state Public Utilities Commissions (PUCs) have significantly less progressive (more regressive) rate structures than local government utilities in the direct-effects model (Model A: Private b = -0.167, p = 0.000). Third, however, the pooled interaction testing whether private PUC-regulated utilities are less responsive to local income inequality than government utilities is statistically null (Model B: Private × Inequality b = -0.209, p = 0.387), despite split-sample results summarized in the abstract and Endnote 17. Because the sole regression outcome (UPR) is a utility-level tariff-design ratio rather than direct household water connection, coverage, service continuity, or household bill-to-income burden, the outcome is an indirect pricing-policy metric (and if UPR is treated as a proxy for basic-volume affordability protection, public vs. private ownership has symmetrical/ambiguous pole orientation while the ownership × inequality interaction is statistically null).
raw_response.specification_or_coding_pitfalls: 1. Utility pricing-structure ratio vs. household water access/affordability burden: The sole regression dependent variable (Unit Price Ratio, UPR) measures tariff-schedule progressivity (unit cost at 30,000 gal/month divided by unit cost at 6,000 gal/month), NOT household piped connection, disconnections, service quality, or household bill-to-income burden. In fact, Table 1 (PDF p. 10) and Endnote 7 (PDF p. 18) show that utilities with regressive declining-block schedules have slightly lower absolute average unit prices at 7,300 gal/month ($5.62/1,000 gal) than utilities with progressive inclining-block schedules ($5.69/1,000 gal) or flat rates ($6.44/1,000 gal), and sample-mean UPR at 30,000 gal/month is 0.91 (< 1.0, slightly regressive due to fixed charges). 2. Formula inversion typo in prose on PDF p. 10: On p. 10 (374), the text verbally describes progressivity as 'the ratio of the average unit price of water at basic consumption levels to the average unit price of water at high volumes' (which would invert the scale), whereas the actual formula used throughout the data and models (p. 11, Table 2 'b ÷ d', Figure 2, Table 3, Figures 4–5) is (average unit price at 30,000 gal) ÷ (average unit price at 6,000 gal), where UPR > 1.0 is progressive and UPR < 1.0 is regressive. 3. Symmetrical ownership coding (sign-flip risk): Table 4 codes Private = 1 (investor-owned, PUC-regulated) vs. 0 (local government-owned), yielding b = -0.167 (p = 0.000) in Model A. Coding private ownership as the exposure gives a negative sign on tariff progressivity, whereas coding public enterprise / local-government ownership as the exposure flips the sign to +0.167. 4. Split-sample narrative vs. null interaction test: The Abstract (p. 1) and Introduction (p. 2) emphasize a significant inequality-progressivity correlation for government utilities and 'no correlation' for private utilities (from subsample regressions noted in Endnote 17), but the formal pooled interaction test in Table 4 Model B (Private × Inequality b = -0.209, p = 0.387) is explicitly not statistically significant (as acknowledged on pp. 15–16). 5. Contextual socioeconomic predictor vs. legal intervention: The headline positive coefficient (b = 0.310, p = 0.005) is for service-area income inequality (mean-to-median income ratio), a demographic context variable rather than a legal or institutional intervention itself.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional observational study of large US drinking water utilities using ordinary least squares (OLS) regression with robust standard errors
raw_response.unit_and_sample_size: Community drinking water utilities in the United States serving populations of 40,000 or more. Sampling frame / descriptive sample: N = 1,189 utilities (1,055 local government-owned utilities and 134 private investor-owned utilities regulated by state PUCs, collectively serving 183,314,934 residents or ~58% of US water utility customers; residential rate schedules collected January–April 2019). Regression analytic sample: N = 1,183 utilities across 218 NOAA climate divisions in the contiguous 48 states (Table 3 and Table 4).
